procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 23rd June, 1981 of the High Court of Bombay in Criminal Appeal No. 1138 and 1144 of 1980.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner was convicted for the offence u/s 302 1.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment by the Sessions Judge. The appeal preferred by him was dismissed by the High Court of Bombay in limine.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner, having had his appeal dismissed summarily by the High Court, approached the Supreme Court by way of a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal, disapproving of the High Court's summary dismissal and directing the High Court to admit the appeal and deal with it according to law.

directions: Set aside the order of the High Court.
The High Court may now 'admit' the appeal and deal with it according to law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power of an appellate court to dismiss an appeal in limine under Section 384 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection, particularly in cases involving serious offenses like murder and a life sentence.

facts: The petitioner was convicted of murder (u/s 302 I.P.C.) and sentenced to life imprisonment by the Sessions Judge.
The petitioner's subsequent appeal to the High Court was dismissed summarily ('in limine') with the single word 'dismissed'.
law: Under Section 384 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appellate court has the power to dismiss an appeal in limine.
Except in cases of guilty pleas and petty offenses, every person convicted of an offense has a statutory right of appeal under the Criminal Procedure Code.
The right of appeal allows a convicted person to ask an appellate court to reappraise the evidence on both facts and law and come to its own conclusion.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the power to dismiss an appeal in limine under Section 384 must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection.

This caution is especially necessary in cases involving serious convictions, such as murder with a life sentence, which are grave enough to warrant a full hearing and independent consideration of the evidence.
The Court held that summarily rejecting such an appeal with a laconic expression like 'dismissed' is a drastic step that is tantamount to denying the convicted person's right of appeal.

The Court also emphasized that appellate courts must provide a 'speaking order' (an order with reasons) when dismissing an appeal in limine to show that the court has addressed the issues and reviewed the record.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the power of an appellate court to dismiss an appeal in limine must be exercised sparingly, particularly in serious cases like murder. A summary dismissal in such a case effectively denies the right of appeal and is improper. Therefore, the High Court's order was set aside, and it was directed to admit the appeal and decide it according to law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the summary rejection of a criminal appeal by the High Court with a laconic, non-speaking order like 'dismissed' is a proper exercise of judicial power, as it can amount to a denial of the right of appeal and impede the Supreme Court's function under Article 136 of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioner was convicted of murder (u/s 302 I.P.C.) and sentenced to life imprisonment by the Sessions Judge.
The petitioner's appeal to the High Court of Bombay was summarily dismissed with the single word 'dismissed'.
law: Under the Criminal Procedure Code (Section 384), an appellate court has the power to dismiss an appeal 'in limine' (at the outset).

Except in cases of guilty pleas or petty offenses, every person convicted of an offense has a right of appeal under the Code, which includes the right to have an appellate court reappraise the evidence on both facts and law.
Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to grant special leave to appeal.
application: The Supreme Court held that the power to dismiss an appeal 'in limine' must be "exercised sparingly and with great circumspection," especially in serious cases like a murder conviction with a life sentence.
The Court reasoned that summarily rejecting such an appeal with a laconic expression like "dismissed" is a "drastic step" that is tantamount to a "denial of right of appeal."

The Court emphasized the necessity of a "speaking order" when dismissing a criminal appeal. Recording reasons, however concise, ensures the proper functioning of the judicial process and shows that the High Court has addressed the issues.
A non-speaking order from the High Court places the Supreme Court in an "embarrassing position" when dealing with a special leave petition under Article 136, as there is no reasoning to review.
The Court noted with disapproval that it had to reiterate this position despite a "long series of judgments" over thirty years correcting the same High Court on this very issue.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court ruled that the summary rejection of a criminal appeal by the High Court with a non-speaking, one-word order like 'dismissed' is an improper exercise of judicial power. It effectively denies the convicted person's right of appeal and hinders the Supreme Court's constitutional function. Therefore, the Court set aside the High Court's order and directed it to admit the appeal and decide it according to law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power of an appellate court to dismiss an appeal in limine under Section 384 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection, particularly in cases involving serious offenses like murder and a life sentence.
appellant_arguments: The power of an appellate court to dismiss an appeal in limine is a power that must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection.
In cases involving serious matters like a murder conviction and a life sentence, summary rejection is a drastic step and the appeal should be admitted for full consideration.
respondent_arguments: The appellate court has the power under Section 384 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to dismiss an appeal in limine. (This argument is inferred as the respondent would be defending the High Court's action, which the Supreme Court acknowledges as an 'undoubted power' before qualifying it).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the summary rejection of a criminal appeal by the High Court with a laconic, non-speaking order like 'dismissed' is a proper exercise of judicial power, as it can amount to a denial of the right of appeal and impede the Supreme Court's function under Article 136 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: Summarily rejecting an appeal with a one-word, non-speaking order like 'dismissed' practically denies the statutory right of appeal.
A convicted person has the right to have an appellate court reappraise the evidence and come to its own conclusion, which requires a reasoned order.
A non-speaking order of dismissal places the Supreme Court in an embarrassing and difficult position when exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's summary dismissal of the appeal was a proper exercise of its judicial power. (This argument is inferred as the respondent's position would be to uphold the legality of the High Court's order).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court's power to dismiss a criminal appeal in limine under Section 384 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection, particularly in serious cases. As a convicted person is entitled to ask an appellate court to reappraise the evidence, it is necessary for the court to provide a speaking order when dismissing a criminal appeal.
obiter: To summarily reject an appeal is to practically deny the right of appeal.
Except in cases where an accused person has pleaded guilty and in petty cases, every person convicted of an offence has a right of appeal under the Code on both facts and law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While an appellate court has the power under Section 384 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to dismiss an appeal in limine, this power must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection. In cases involving serious convictions like murder with a life sentence, a summary rejection with a laconic, non-speaking order like 'dismissed' is a drastic step that practically denies the statutory right of appeal. An appellate court must issue a speaking order, however concise, to show it has applied its mind to the issues.
legal_tests_applied: The power to dismiss an appeal in limine under Section 384 of the Criminal Procedure Code must be exercised sparingly and with great circumspection.
In cases involving serious convictions (e.g., murder and life imprisonment), the gravity of the matter itself warrants admission of the appeal for full and independent consideration of the evidence.
An appellate court must make a speaking order when dismissing a criminal appeal in limine to demonstrate that it addressed the questions at issue and had the record before it.
policy_considerations: To summarily reject a serious criminal appeal with a one-word order is to 'practically deny the right of appeal' that every convicted person (barring certain exceptions) has under the Code.
A convicted person is entitled to have an appellate court reappraise the evidence and come to its own conclusion, a right which is nullified by a non-speaking summary dismissal.

The absence of a reasoned order from the High Court places the Supreme Court in a 'most embarrassing position' when exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, as it cannot ascertain the basis for the dismissal.
The 'requirement of recording reasons for summary dismissal, however concise, serves to ensure proper functioning of the judicial process.'
